extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, administrative law practitioners, legislators, and regulators implementing or complying with the Administrative Procedure Act
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for agency rulemaking, investigations, hearings, evidence, decisions, subpoenas, and ancillary procedural rights under the Administrative Procedure Act and its implementing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of prosecuting and adjudicative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must reflect separation of functions in organization and procedure; top authority should not reserve both prosecuting and deciding functions and should delegate supervision of investigations and initiation of cases to responsible subordinate officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The top authority is ultimately responsible for all functions but "may and should confine itself to determining policy and delegate the actual supervision of investigations and initiation of cases to responsible subordinate officers." Agencies (e.g., heads of bureaus or departments) performing mainly executive functions should delegate at least the initial decision of cases to examiners or boards of examiners and confine their own review to important issues of law or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited applicability of statutory exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory exemptions (e.g., ex parte matters, applications for initial licenses, cases consolidated with rulemaking like rates/facilities) should be interpreted narrowly and not applied where matters are accusatory or involve sharply controverted factual issues requiring fair procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemptions such as for 'ex parte matters authorized by law' or initial license applications free some matters from section requirements, but agencies should not apply these exceptions in instances tending to be accusatory or involving sharply controverted factual issues because exceptions are not to be interpreted as precluding fair procedure where it is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory adjudications in sound discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency authorized to hold hearings may, in its sound discretion, issue declaratory orders with the same effect as other orders, subject to statutory limitations and judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such orders may be issued only where the agency is empowered by statute to hold hearings and the subject is not otherwise exempted; agencies are not required to issue them on request; they do not bind nonparties or determine unpresented subject matter; issuance is governed by principles similar to judicial declaratory judgments and is reviewable like other orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancillary provisions not to override contrary statutory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions relating to incidental or miscellaneous rights, powers, and procedures (section 6) do not override contrary provisions elsewhere in the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introductory exception 'except as otherwise provided in this act' limits section 6 rights (for example, the right of appearance) so as not to authorize improper ex parte conferences during formal hearings and pending formal decisions under sections 7 and 8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of appearance and counsel (Section 6(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person compelled to appear in person before an agency or its representative is entitled to counsel; every party may appear in person or by counsel; interested persons may appear before responsible officers 'so far as the orderly conduct of public business permits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must proceed with reasonable dispatch to conclude matters presented and must not create burdensome requirements for lawyers in good standing; the subsection neither recognizes nor denies the propriety of nonlawyers representing parties but preserves the right of agencies to pass upon qualifications of nonlawyers and not permit unauthorized practice of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and requirements for administrative investigations (Section 6(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative process must be authorized by law, substantially and demonstrably necessary to agency operations, conducted through authorized representatives, and confined to the legal and factual sphere of the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations must not be 'fishing expeditions,' must avoid disturbing personal privacy or unreasonably interfering with private occupation or enterprise, and should interfere to the least degree compatible with adequate law enforcement. Persons compelled to submit evidence are entitled to retain or procure copies (with cost) except in nonpublic proceedings where inspection of the official transcript may be limited for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to transcripts in nonpublic investigatory proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: In nonpublic (grand jury–type) investigatory proceedings, witnesses may, for good cause, be limited to inspection of the official transcript rather than given copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cause must be clear and convincing when limiting copies (e.g., when later prosecutions would be nullified by circulating copies). Parties should generally have copies or an opportunity for inspection to ensure correctness and to use in other proceedings; limitation is narrowly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative subpoenas: availability and judicial review (Section 6(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where authorized by law, agencies may issue subpoenas; parties may secure subpoenas upon request and a showing of general relevance and reasonable scope, subject to agency rules, and may contest validity in court prior to penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision assures private parties the same access to subpoenas as agency representatives, prevents improvident subpoenas and burdensome showings, and imposes a statutory limitation on subpoenas exceeding agency authority. Courts, upon contest, should inquire generally into legal and factual situation and determine relevant questions of law, issuing enforcement orders when subpoenas conform to law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt notice of agency denials and statement of grounds (Section 6(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must give prompt notice of denials of requests in any proceeding, accompanied by a brief statement of procedural or other grounds sufficient to apprise the party of the basis of the denial and available administrative remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A self‑explanatory denial or an affirming of a prior denial satisfies the requirement only if the grounds previously stated remain the actual grounds and sufficiently notify the party; the statement must enable the party to determine further remedies or recourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings apply only where statutorily required and are supplementary (Section 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal hearing provisions (section 7) apply only where other statutes require hearings and are supplementary to the settlement provisions of sections 5 and 6(a); hearings must not be used as indirect burdens or penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are to be given every opportunity to simplify or settle cases; hearings are not required unless statute so provides and functional exceptions in section 5 are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presiding officers must act impartially and may be disqualified (Section 7(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings must be held by the agency, its members, examiners, or other specially provided officers; all presiding officers must operate impartially and may withdraw or be disqualified on proper affidavit of bias, with the agency deciding the matter as part of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding officers are subject to the bill's provisions, must conduct hearings 'in a strictly impartial and considerate manner,' ensure necessary evidence is adduced, keep hearings orderly and efficient, and must not proceed in willful disregard of law. Bias or disqualification decided on the record becomes subject to administrative and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorities of presiding officers (Section 7(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Presiding officers have authority (subject to agency rules and powers) to administer oaths; issue authorized subpoenas; receive evidence and rule on offers of proof; take or cause depositions; regulate the hearing; hold settlement/simplification conferences; dispose of procedural requests; make decisions or recommended decisions under section 8; and exercise other consistent authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list assures presiding officers perform real adjudicative functions rather than merely clerical roles; the agency that ultimately decides should not conduct hearings 'from behind the scenes' without knowledge of hearing room proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards and burden of proof (Section 7(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The proponent of a rule or order bears the burden of proof; agencies must exclude irrelevant, immaterial, or unduly repetitious evidence and may impose no sanction or issue no rule or order except upon the whole record or cited portions supported by 'reliable, probative, and substantial evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any party may present oral or documentary evidence, rebuttal evidence, and conduct reasonable cross‑examination. Agencies cannot arbitrarily disbelieve credible, credited evidence; where evidence is pro and con agencies must weigh it and decide according to preponderance; admission of technical reports, surveys, analyses, and summaries is permitted where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑examination and written evidence limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross‑examination is not unlimited; presiding officers must determine whether cross‑examination is pushed to unreasonable lengths or is required for 'full and true disclosure of the facts.' Agencies may adopt written‑submission procedures (especially in rulemaking or initial license proceedings) provided no party's interest is prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written technical data may be introduced and, where cross‑examination is necessary to bring out truth, the party must have it. Adequate opportunity to prepare and submit rebuttal evidence must be provided. The test for limiting cross‑examination is necessity for full disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of hearings and official notice (Section 7(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of evidence taken and papers filed is exclusive for decision and, upon payment of costs, available to parties. If decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the record, any party may, on timely request, show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official notice may be taken only of generally recognized, ordinarily indisputable facts (scientific or public in nature). Where agencies take such notice they must state it on the record or in decisions and afford an opportunity to contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial decisions, recommended decisions, and agency review (Section 8(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency did not preside, the presiding officer must make the initial decision unless the agency chooses to make the initial decision; initial decisions become agency decisions in absence of appeal. If the agency makes an initial decision without presiding, the officer who took evidence must make a recommended decision (with certain exceptions for rulemaking or initial licenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners' initial or recommended decisions become part of the record and are consequential (e.g., credibility determinations). Agencies must prescribe a reasonable time for appeals from examiners' decisions; when reviewing, agencies should specify issues of law, fact, or discretion for review with particularity. In exceptional circumstances the agency may issue tentative decisions or omit intermediate procedures if found imperative on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for submittals and content of decisions (Section 8(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to any recommended or other decision or review, parties must be given opportunity to submit proposed findings and conclusions, exceptions to recommended decisions, and supporting reasons; the record must show rulings on each such submission. All recommended or other decisions must include findings and conclusions and reasons on all material issues and state appropriate agency action or denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefs on law and facts must be received and fully considered; oral argument must be heard when required by law or where issues are serious. Findings need not be long but must be sufficient to relate issues of fact, law, and discretion to the record; credibility findings should be made when material. Decisions must be served on named parties and furnished to participants and interested persons who request them.

rubrics_metrics.name: No sanction or rule beyond delegated jurisdiction (Section 9(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may impose no sanction or issue any substantive rule or order except within the jurisdiction delegated to it and as authorized by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general limitation applies to the exercise of any power or authority by an agency and is meant to ensure agencies act only within statutory authority.
